newsitem.title: USA: Ford CEO Trotman's 1996 pay rises 5.7 pct.
newsitem.headline: Ford CEO Trotman's 1996 pay rises 5.7 pct.

text.p: Ford Motor Co Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Alex Trotman earned total compensation of $5,738,976 during 1996, a 5.7 percent increase over his 1995 compensation of $5,431,354, the automaker said Monday in its annual proxy statement.
Ford said Trotman's base salary increased to $1,916,667 in 1996 from $1,500,000 in 1995, marking Trotman's first increase in base pay since he took over as Ford chairman in 1993.
But Trotman's bonus award fell 16.7 percent to $2.5 million in 1996 from $3 million in 1995.
Half of Trotman's 1996 bonus has already been paid, but the remainder is deferred until his retirement and is at risk because it is tied to Ford's stock performance, the company said.

In 1995, 60 percent of Trotman's $3 million bonus was deferred until his retirement and also was tied to Ford's stock price. Ford's board of directors recently voted to extend Trotman's employment with the company until January 1, 2000, delaying his retirement by about two years past age 65.
Included in Trotman's $5.7 million total for 1996 is an award of restricted stock worth $700,429 that is generally available to him until 18 months after his retirement.
In 1995, Trotman received a restricted stock award worth $456,444.

Of his total 1996 compensation, $3,669,551 is available to him now and $2,069,425 is deferred until after his retirement and is tied to the long-term performance of the company and the future value of Ford stock.

Not included in Trotman's 1996 compensation total is his exercising of stock appreciation rights totaling $1,323,215. Ford officials said the rights are the equivalent of exercising stock options and immediately selling the shares.
The stock rights bring Trotman's total income for 1996 to $7,062,191. He did not exercise any options in 1995.

Also not included in Trotman's 1996 total are new options to purchase 300,000 shares of Ford common stock at a price of $32.69 each. Ford estimated that those options have a present-day value of $2,079,000.
However, the option price is currently higher than Ford's stock price, which was unchanged at 30-7/8 on Monday morning.
In 1995, Trotman received options for 350,000 shares at $32 each, valued at the time at $2,516,500.

Ford also disclosed for the first time Monday that Trotman earned $1,260,000 in the form of restricted stock in 1995 under a long-term incentive payout. The payout for 1996 will not be determined until mid-1997, and will not be disclosed until Ford releases next year's proxy statement. The stock is restricted until after he retires.
Ford said bonuses were lower for nearly all top executives because the general bonus pool for 1996 fell to $169 million from $192 million in 1995.
The bonus pool fell because the amount of capital employed in the business rose for 1996.

Ford Automotive Operations President Jacques Nasser was the only top executive to receive a higher bonus -- with the amount increasing to $950,000 from $850,000 in 1995. Ford officials said the increase was due largely to his promotion last October to his current job.
